t: Aim and plan of the session
n: The topic of this session: detection of procaine, tetracaine, lidocaine and diphenhydramine in an extract, with quantitative analysis carried out by the PEC method, that is photoelectrocolorimetry. The aim is for you to master the use of these substances, poisoning cases and metabolism, and the methods of isolating them from physical evidence and analysing them. According to the plan, we will consider in turn the toxicological significance and the methods of analysis of procaine, tetracaine, lidocaine and diphenhydramine.

By the end of the session, students become familiar with the specific methods of isolating procaine, tetracaine, lidocaine and diphenhydramine. They master the toxicological significance of the substances, qualitative and quantitative analysis, and methods of detection. In the practical part the azo dye reaction, the microcrystalline reaction with Dragendorff reagent and colour reactions are performed. You draw the shape of the resulting microcrystals in the work notebook.

Items needed for the work: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual aids. The session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. For the azo dye reaction a porcelain dish and starch-iodide paper are needed. For microcrystalloscopy a microscope slide, a humid chamber and a microscope are used. For thin-layer chromatography, KSK and Silufol plates are taken, and for PEC, light filters are selected.

Now the reagents. For procaine you need 1% HCl, 1% sodium nitrite, 2% sodium hydroxide, an alkaline solution of β-naphthol and Dragendorff reagent. For tetracaine, concentrated HNO3 and alkali are used, that is the Vitali-Morin reaction, as well as 30% sodium nitrite and 0.1 M HCl. For diphenhydramine, concentrated H2SO4, a mixture of H2SO4 and HNO3, Marquis, Liebermann and Mandelin reagents, and acid chromotrope blue are prepared.

Rules of safety and preparation. For the laboratory work the student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed when the work is finished. Objects from infected persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis and AIDS, arrive in a special container and must be noted in the documents.

Let us look at the classification of the substances. Procaine is an ester of p-aminobenzoic acid with diethylaminoethanol. Tetracaine is an ester of p-butylaminobenzoic acid with dimethylaminoethanol. Diphenhydramine is a compound of the β-dimethylaminoethyl benzhydrol ether type. In addition, lidocaine hydrochloride is also analysed in this session. That is, in structure procaine and tetracaine are close to one family, while diphenhydramine belongs to the benzhydrol ether type.

Procaine is a synthetic compound used in place of natural cocaine. To overcome cocainism, procaine and tetracaine were synthesised. Chemically, procaine is an ester of p-aminobenzoic acid with diethylaminoethanol, and occurs as a white crystalline powder. It dissolves well in water and ethyl alcohol, and poorly in chloroform and ether. In medicine procaine is used as a local analgesic.

Let us compare procaine and tetracaine. Procaine acts more weakly than cocaine. Tetracaine, however, is 2 times stronger than cocaine and 10 times stronger than procaine. Both were synthesised to overcome the toxic action of cocaine, that is cocainism. Tetracaine is used for anaesthesia in bronchoscopy and oesophagoscopy and in ophthalmology. As the table shows, procaine is a white crystalline powder, while tetracaine is a white or yellow crystalline substance.

Toxicological significance of procaine. Some people are very sensitive to procaine. In poisoning, dizziness, weakness, lowered blood pressure, collapse and shock are observed. In a toxic dose, excitation of nervous activity occurs first, then paralysis of the central nervous system. In the body procaine breaks down into p-aminobenzoic acid and diethylaminoethanol, and about 2% is excreted unchanged in the urine.

Let us go through the metabolic pathway of procaine in sequence. Procaine entering the body breaks down, forming p-aminobenzoic acid and diethylaminoethanol. About 2% of the substance is excreted unchanged in the urine. Therefore procaine itself can also be found in urine. Remember that in a toxic dose, excitation is observed first, then paralysis of the central nervous system.

The azo dye reaction of procaine. The residue is dissolved in 1 ml of 1% HCl. Then 1% NaNO2 is added until starch-iodide paper turns blue. After 5 minutes the medium is made alkaline with 2% NaOH and 1-2 drops of alkaline β-naphthol are added. As a result a red colour or precipitate forms. The scheme shows this sequence step by step.

Pay attention to the reaction scheme. Under the action of sodium nitrite and β-naphthol, a procaine solution forms a red azo dye. If there is a lot of the substance, a red precipitate settles. Nitrite is added until starch-iodide paper turns blue, and after 5 minutes the medium is made alkaline. The reaction starts from procaine in 1% HCl, and the conditions must be followed exactly.

Dragendorff and ultraviolet spectrum methods for procaine. To the residue 1-2 drops of Dragendorff reagent are added and it is kept for 15-20 minutes in a humid chamber, which gives rectangular crystals. In the ultraviolet spectrum the aqueous solution absorbs at a maximum of 290 nm. A solution in 0.2 M sulphuric acid gives maxima at 228, 272 and 279 nm. The table gives the methods and results side by side.

Let us sum up the main indicators of procaine. The aqueous solution gives a maximum at 290 nm, the solution in 0.2 M sulphuric acid at 228, 272 and 279 nm. In thin-layer chromatography of urine on a KSK plate, in the cyclohexane-benzene-diethylamine 75:25:10 system, a brown spot with Rf=0.16-0.18 forms. In the microcrystalline reaction, Dragendorff reagent is kept for 15-20 minutes in a humid chamber. 2% is found unchanged in urine.

Detecting procaine in urine. To 5 ml of urine, 1% HCl is added, then 1% NaNO2 until starch-iodide paper turns blue. After 5 minutes, 2% NaOH and β-naphthol are added. If procaine is present, the solution turns red-brown. In the microcrystalline method, two drops of urine are slowly dried on a microscope slide and Dragendorff reagent is added. As a result red-brown rectangular crystals form.

Detecting procaine by thin-layer chromatography. Drops of urine and a "witness" solution, 2-3 cm apart, are applied to the start line of a KSK plate. The plate is developed in the cyclohexane-benzene-diethylamine 75:25:10 system and dried. Then Munier-Dragendorff reagent is sprayed on. Procaine gives a brown spot, with an Rf value of 0.16-0.18. The witness solution serves for comparison of the result.

The PEC method for procaine. Photocolorimetry is based on measuring the substance in the visible part of the spectrum under polychromatic radiation. The absorption maximum of the coloured solution must coincide with the absorption minimum of the light filter. For the authenticity analysis, the azo dye reaction is carried out in the order given above, and the maximum absorption is measured with different light filters. The light filter is selected and the results are recorded in the work notebook. The amount of procaine is determined by PEC on the basis of the azo dye reaction.

The stages of PEC analysis are as follows. First, the azo dye reaction is carried out to confirm the authenticity of procaine. Then the absorption of the solution is measured with different light filters. The light filter is selected so that the maximum of the solution coincides with the minimum of the light filter. Finally, the results are written in the work notebook. Remember: photocolorimetry is based on measuring the substance in the visible part of the spectrum under polychromatic radiation.

Tetracaine is an ester of p-butylaminobenzoic acid with dimethylaminoethanol, a white or yellow crystalline substance. It is highly toxic: 2 times stronger than cocaine and 10 times stronger than procaine. The signs of poisoning resemble those of cocaine. Tetracaine is extracted with organic solvents from an alkaline medium. It is used for anaesthesia in bronchoscopy and oesophagoscopy and in ophthalmology.

Potency and detection indicators of tetracaine. Tetracaine is highly toxic, acting 2 times more strongly than cocaine and 10 times more strongly than procaine. In the Vitali-Morin reaction a red colour forms. With 30% NaNO2, after 15-20 minutes, thin crystals cut in two appear. In the ultraviolet spectrum in 0.1 M H2SO4 the maxima are observed at 229, 281 and 312 nm.

Qualitative reactions of tetracaine. Like atropine, tetracaine gives the Vitali-Morin reaction and forms a red colour. For the microcrystalline reaction the residue is dissolved in 0.1 M HCl, 1 drop of 30% NaNO2 is added, and after 15-20 minutes thin crystals cut in two form. In the ultraviolet spectrum in 0.1 M H2SO4 there are maxima at 229, 281 and 312 nm. The table summarises these results.

Lidocaine, that is xylocaine. Lidocaine hydrochloride is a white or yellowish crystalline powder. It dissolves readily in water, 95% alcohol and acetone, and does not dissolve in ether. It melts at 128-129 °C. It is unstable in light and, on prolonged standing, oxidises and turns yellow. With cobalt nitrate it gives a blue-green crystalline precipitate, and in the ultraviolet spectrum it absorbs at a maximum at 235-269 nm.

Main indicators of lidocaine. Lidocaine hydrochloride is a white crystalline powder with a bitter taste. It dissolves readily in water, 95% alcohol and acetone, and does not dissolve in ether. Its melting point is 128-129 °C. On prolonged exposure to light it oxidises and turns yellow. In ultraviolet spectrophotometry it absorbs at a maximum at 235-269 nm. Remember also that it forms a blue-green precipitate with cobalt nitrate.

Toxicological significance of lidocaine. The excitability of the central nervous system increases, with severe headache, euphoria, drowsiness and photophobia. Hearing deteriorates, the lips and tongue are paralysed, and paralysis of the respiratory muscles may occur. Body temperature falls, and shivering and severe cardiac insufficiency, that is collapse, develop. In addition, allergic reactions are observed: itching, swelling and erythema.

Let us divide the signs of lidocaine poisoning into groups. The first group is the central nervous system: excitability increases, with severe headache, euphoria, drowsiness and photophobia. The second group is paralysis: hearing deteriorates, and the lips, tongue and respiratory muscles are paralysed. The third group is the heart and body: temperature falls, with shivering and collapse. The fourth group is allergic reactions, manifesting as itching, swelling and erythema.

Diphenhydramine is a β-dimethylaminoethyl benzhydrol ether, a fine white crystalline powder with a bitter taste, which numbs the tongue. It dissolves well in water, 95% ethyl alcohol and chloroform, poorly in acetone, and does not dissolve in ether. It is an antihistamine agent. Because it potentiates the action of narcotic and psychotropic substances, it is widely abused by drug addicts and toxicomaniacs. About 2-4% is excreted unchanged in the urine, with an average elimination period of 3-10 hours.

Let us classify the actions of diphenhydramine. Diphenhydramine is an active antihistamine agent, used as injections and tablets. It also has local anaesthetic, muscle-relaxant and antispasmodic action. On the nervous system it has neuroleptic and hypnotic action, and there is also an antiemetic action. Because it potentiates the action of barbiturates, narcotic and psychotropic substances, it is widely abused by drug addicts.

t: Isolating diphenhydramine from blood and urine
n: Procedure for isolating diphenhydramine from blood and urine. 10 ml of urine or 2 ml of blood is brought to pH=10 with ammonia and extracted twice with chloroform. It is then passed through a filter with anhydrous Na2SO4. For GLC, the organic solvent is evaporated to a small residue, that is to 0.5 ml. For quantitative analysis it is evaporated to a dry residue.

Chromatographic purification of diphenhydramine and thin-layer chromatography. On a Silufol plate the chloroform-acetone-ammonia 12:24:1 system is used, and the solution is run to a height of 10 cm. When concentrated H2SO4 is sprayed on, diphenhydramine gives a yellow spot, Rf 0.58-0.60. Its metabolite benzhydrol forms a spot at Rf=0.76-0.80. In the table the two substances are compared by Rf value and spot colour.

Kinetics and chromatographic indicators of diphenhydramine. Diphenhydramine leaves the body in an average of 3-10 hours, and about 2-4% is excreted unchanged in the urine. In thin-layer chromatography diphenhydramine gives Rf=0.58-0.60 and a yellow spot, and its metabolite benzhydrol has Rf=0.76-0.80. For extraction, blood or urine is brought to pH=10 with ammonia.

Colour reactions of diphenhydramine. With concentrated H2SO4 a yellow colour forms, then it turns red-brick; when water is added the colour disappears. With a mixture of H2SO4 and HNO3 a red colour appears; when water is added, brown, yellow and orange colours appear, and the chloroform turns violet. According to the table, Marquis reagent gives lemon yellow, Liebermann reagent orange, and Mandelin reagent yellow.

Let us remember the three reagents for diphenhydramine separately. Under the action of Marquis reagent a lemon-yellow colour forms. Under the action of Liebermann reagent an orange colour forms. Under the action of Mandelin reagent, if the residue contains diphenhydramine, a yellow colour forms. Concentrated H2SO4 gives a yellow colour, which then turns red-brick.

The reaction of diphenhydramine with H2SO4 and HNO3. If a mixture of concentrated sulphuric and nitric acids acts on the residue, a red colour forms. If water is added gradually to the coloured product, first a brown, then a yellow and orange colour appears. If chloroform is added to the last product and shaken, the chloroform layer turns violet. This observation is recorded as a sign characteristic of diphenhydramine.

t: Diphenhydramine: UV spectrum and quantitative analysis
n: Ultraviolet spectrum and quantitative analysis of diphenhydramine. Its solution in 0.1 M sulphuric acid absorbs at a maximum at 252 and 257 nm. Quantitative analysis is based on the stable colour formed with acid chromotrope blue. The residue is dissolved in 1 ml of 0.1 M HCl, 10 ml of chloroform is added, then 6.4 ml of indicator, and the volume is made up to 20 ml. It is shaken for 3 minutes and the chloroform layer is measured at 567 nm.

Steps of the quantitative analysis of diphenhydramine. The analysis is based on the stable colour formed with the indicator acid chromotrope blue, which is stable in an acidic medium. The dry residue is dissolved in 1 ml of 0.1 M HCl, and 10 ml of chloroform and 6.4 ml of indicator are added. The indicator is taken as an aqueous solution of 2.63 g/l. The volume is made up to 20 ml and shaken for 3 minutes. The chloroform layer is measured at 567 nm in a 10 mm cuvette. The standard scale consists of 0.05-0.3 mg of diphenhydramine.

Now a situational problem. The blood and urine of Z. Sharipov, born in 1976, were brought to the forensic chemistry department in 2 brown glass containers of 200 ml each. In the urine the azo dye reaction gave a red-brown colour. With Dragendorff reagent, red-brown rectangular crystals formed. Question: to which substance does the poison in the blood and urine samples belong, and write the reaction equation.

Let us consider the chain of evidence in the problem. When the urine was reacted with HCl, NaNO2 and β-naphthol, it gave a red-brown colour. With Dragendorff reagent, red-brown rectangular crystals formed. These signs correspond to the reactions given in the book for procaine. Therefore, as a conclusion, the signs of procaine are recorded.

Case 22. In blood and urine, the signs of poisoning resemble those of cocaine; for which substance must analysis be carried out? In poisoning with tetracaine, the same signs appear as in poisoning with cocaine. Procaine, however, acts more weakly than cocaine, and tetracaine is 2 times stronger than cocaine. For tetracaine, a red colour in the Vitali-Morin reaction and cut crystals with NaNO2 are characteristic. For procaine, a red azo dye and rectangular crystals with Dragendorff reagent are characteristic.

Review questions. First: name the substances that are derivatives of p-aminobenzoic acid and write their formulae. Second: explain the reactions that form microcrystals and a coloured product with procaine; how is procaine determined in urine by thin-layer chromatography? Third: which colour reaction is used in detecting tetracaine, with which reagent does it form microcrystals, and what are its physicochemical methods? Fourth: how are the amounts of procaine and tetracaine determined; how is diphenhydramine isolated from urine and how is it analysed?

Conclusion. Procaine: a red colour or precipitate in the azo dye reaction, rectangular crystals with Dragendorff reagent, Rf=0.16-0.18 in urine by thin-layer chromatography. Tetracaine: the Vitali-Morin reaction gives red, crystals form with 30% NaNO2, and in the ultraviolet spectrum 229, 281, 312 nm. Lidocaine: a blue-green precipitate with cobalt nitrate. Diphenhydramine: Rf 0.58-0.60 yellow spot, Marquis reagent lemon yellow, in the ultraviolet spectrum 252 and 257 nm; the amount is determined at 567 nm with acid chromotrope blue.
